subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Parvovirus B19 is a small, non‑enveloped ssDNA virus that infects erythroid precursors, causing a two‑stage illness: a brief febrile viremia followed by a rash/arthralgia phase. It can trigger aplastic crises in patients with chronic hemolysis or fetal hydrops in pregnancy.

sections.p: Parvovirus B19 is the only human pathogenic member of the genus Parvovirus. It spreads by respiratory droplets and has a single serotype, making immunity lifelong after infection.
b: Smallest known DNA virus (≈5 kb)
Non‑enveloped, icosahedral capsid
Peak incidence in late winter‑spring

sections.p: The virus binds the P antigen on erythroid progenitors, enters the nucleus, and replicates using host DNA polymerase, causing cell lysis and transient arrest of red‑cell production.
b: ssDNA, linear, single‑strand
Requires dividing erythroid cells for replication
Only one serotype → no antigenic variation

sections.p: Transmission is mainly via respiratory secretions; after a 4‑day incubation the virus enters the bloodstream, infects bone‑marrow erythroid precursors, and is cleared when IgG appears.
b: Contagious during the febrile viremia phase only
IgM appears ~10 days, IgG confers lasting immunity

sections.p: Two clinical phases: (1) infectious febrile illness with high‑titer viremia; (2) immune‑mediated rash/arthralgia after antibodies develop. In high‑risk hosts it can cause pure red‑cell aplasia or fetal hydrops.
b: Erythema infectiosum (slapped‑cheek rash) in children
Arthropathy in adults, often symmetric hands/feet
Aplastic crisis in sickle‑cell disease or chronic hemolysis
Fetal hydrops, miscarriage, or intrauterine death if infection occurs in pregnancy

sections.p: Combine clinical pattern with specific laboratory tests; serology is the mainstay, but PCR is useful when antibodies are absent or immunosuppression is present.
b: If PCR unavailable, rely on IgM/IgG pattern and clinical picture.

t.b: Is the patient in the acute phase? Positive IgM confirms recent infection; negative IgM with positive IgG indicates past exposure.
Has the patient developed immunity? Positive IgG shows prior infection or immunity; useful for counseling pregnant women.
Is there active viral replication? Detects virus when serology is equivocal, especially in immunocompromised patients.
Is there an aplastic crisis? Sudden drop in hemoglobin with reticulocytopenia points to B19‑mediated marrow suppression.

sections.p: Supportive care is primary; treat anemia in aplastic crisis and consider IVIG for severe immunocompromised infection. Prevent spread by isolating contagious patients.
b: Red‑cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia or aplastic crisis
IVIG (pooled immunoglobulin) for chronic infection in immunodeficiency
No specific antiviral; ribavirin not routinely used
Isolation until fever resolves and viremia clears (≈1 week)

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical reasoning.
b: Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid precursors → pure red‑cell aplasia.
Contagious period ends when IgM appears; rash phase is non‑infectious.
In sickle‑cell disease, a sudden drop in hemoglobin with low reticulocytes = aplastic crisis → test for B19.

whenToSeekHelp: Fetal hydrops or unexplained miscarriage in a pregnant woman
Persistent fever and pancytopenia in an immunocompromised patient

faq.q: Why does the rash appear after the fever?
faq.a: The rash coincides with antibody formation; immune complexes deposit in skin, causing the characteristic erythema.
Adults rarely develop the classic facial rash; they more often present with arthralgia or a mild flu‑like illness.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for Parvovirus B19?
faq.a: No vaccine exists; prevention relies on hygiene and avoiding close contact during the contagious phase.

exam: Describe the two clinical phases of Parvovirus B19 infection and their pathophysiologic basis.
A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden anemia and reticulocytopenia. Which test confirms the cause and what is the management?
Explain why a pregnant woman infected in the first trimester is at risk for fetal hydrops.
